items.name: ch9
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices funny cartoon characters (a cheeky time-traveller, khans, princes, tsars, servants, nobles, officers, an empress): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags.
lines: Scientists sliced his brain into thousands of thin pieces, looking for the secret of his genius. His body was preserved and put on display in Red Square, where it still lies today.
[grimacing] They didn't find the genius. They did find a lot of brain.
Before he died, Lenin had warned the party: Joseph Stalin was too rude and too powerful, and should be removed.
By the end of the nineteen-twenties, Stalin had outplayed every rival. The biggest, Leon Trotsky, was thrown out of the country, hunted down in Mexico... and killed with an ice axe.
Stalin wanted to turn a country of peasants into an industrial superpower in about ten years.
So he forced farmers off their own land and onto giant state farms. Those who resisted were shot, or sent to labour camps: the Gulag.
Grain was taken away even as people starved. In nineteen thirty-two and thirty-three, millions died in a famine. Ukraine suffered the most. Ukrainians call it the Holodomor: death by hunger.
Then Stalin turned on everyone else. In nineteen thirty-seven and thirty-eight, his secret police arrested around one and a half million people, and shot around seven hundred thousand of them.
Generals. Scientists. Poets. Ordinary people, reported by their own neighbours.
And some didn't just disappear from life. They disappeared from photos.
[holding up a photo] Comrade. Who is this man next to Comrade Stalin?
[brushing furiously] I see only Comrade Stalin. And a very beautiful canal.
That man was Nikolai Yezhov, the secret police boss who had run the killings. After he was shot himself, he was painted out of the photo, leaving Stalin alone by the water.
[pointing back] Remember the dictator who erased people from photos? That's him.
In nineteen thirty-nine, Stalin shocked the world. He signed a deal with his sworn enemy, Adolf Hitler. They promised not to attack each other, and secretly split Eastern Europe between them.
Stalin trusted it. His spies warned him, again and again, that Germany was coming. He ignored them.
On June the twenty-second, nineteen forty-one, more than three million German and allied soldiers invaded. Three giant pushes: towards Leningrad, towards Moscow, and into the south.
The largest invasion in human history. And the Red Army, gutted by Stalin's own purges, collapsed.
Leningrad, Peter the Great's city, was surrounded for nearly nine hundred days. People boiled leather belts and wallpaper paste just to have something to eat. Around a million civilians died.
The Germans reached the edge of Moscow. And then... winter arrived. Again.
[to camera] Rule number one. Still: don't.
Then came Stalingrad: the city named after Stalin himself. For months, the two armies fought street by street, sometimes room by room.
In the end, a whole German army was surrounded and forced to surrender. After that, Germany never stopped going backwards.
In nineteen forty-five, Soviet soldiers raised the red flag over Berlin.
The cost is almost impossible to imagine. Around twenty-seven million Soviet people died. Almost every family lost someone.
Stalin came out of the war ruling half of Europe. By nineteen forty-nine, he had the atomic bomb.
And in nineteen fifty-three, his death might have been the most Stalin thing of all.
[whispering] He hasn't come out all day.
You knock. The last man who woke him up is in Siberia.
When they finally went in, he was lying on the floor. And good doctors were hard to find, because many of the country's top doctors had just been arrested, in a plot Stalin himself had invented.
He died a few days later. The man who terrified a whole country died, at least partly, because everyone was too terrified to help him.
